sections.h2: Where to pay and who to call
sections.html:
Forsyth County Tax Administration values real and personal property and collects the county levy. Visit the Government Center at 201 North Chestnut Street, Winston-Salem, any weekday from 8 in the morning until 5 in the afternoon, or call 336-703-2300.

Send mail to Forsyth County Tax Collector, PO Box 82, Winston-Salem, NC 27102. There is a drop box by the parking deck entrance that accepts payments at any hour, and phone and online payment are available too. Credit cards add 2.25 percent with a $2.00 minimum, debit cards add $2.85 and an e-check adds $.20 up to $9,999.99.

For fiscal year 2027 the county charges 55.40 cents on every $100 of assessed value, an increase of 1.88 cents over the prior year. Towns and fire districts layer their own levy over that figure. Property tax covers 61 percent of county revenue, so the budget drives the rate.

The rate sheet names ten places in all: Winston-Salem, High Point, Kernersville, King, Clemmons, Lewisville, Rural Hall, Walkertown, Tobaccoville and Bethania. Clemmons, Lewisville, Bethania and Tobaccoville carry extra fire district and local columns, so the total depends on the parcel's fire district. Winston-Salem also has a business improvement district with an extra levy.

Bills are due September 1 and can be paid without penalty through January 5. After that, interest starts at 2 percent for January and goes up by three-fourths of one percent each month.

A bill is delinquent once January 5 arrives with the September 1 charge still open. Garnishment of wages and levy on personal property may start immediately. The office can also intercept state income tax refunds and lottery winnings through debt setoff. A mailed payment counts on its USPS postmark date, and a date from a private postage meter does not substitute.

Electronic payments count when the money reaches the collector, not when you click submit. E-checks take several days, and a wrong account number gets the payment rejected, which can push you past due. Owners who have fallen behind can ask a revenue collector for a payment agreement, and current owners can start a prepayment plan in January.

Every real property value was reset as of January 1, 2025. In the county's words the figure is its estimate of what the parcel would likely sell for on that day.

Eight years is the legal maximum between reappraisals, yet Forsyth has generally moved every four years since 1988 to soften swings. Notices went out in the first two weeks of February 2025. One property can rise or fall independently of its neighbors, and the change in a bill depends on the new value, any personal property you own and the rate. The rate is set separately, usually in May or June.

Start with an informal appeal to Tax Administration. When that leaves the question open, put a written request in front of the Board of Equalization and Review.

  • Formal window: January 1 through June 30 unless the county advertises another period, or 15 days after the latest value notice if that falls later.
  • Form: print the board's appeal form from the parcel's detail page, or call 336-703-2300 and the office will send one.
  • Personal property: a written appeal is due 30 days after the first notice or bill.
  • Next level: the North Carolina Property Tax Commission hears a board decision when notice is filed inside the 30 days set by G.S. 105-290. The state courts sit above it.

Reappraisal appraisers are often out of the office, so call first and leave a number for a callback, or book an appointment. Informal appeals can also be filed online through the county's eNotices portal.

The office takes applications for three state programs, each due by June 1, and an owner may use only one.

  • Owners who are elderly or disabled and earn $38,800 or less for 2026 can exclude $25,000 of value, or half the value if that is bigger.
  • A disabled veteran excludes $45,000 on a residence, using Form AV-9 and VA certification of a permanent and total service-connected disability.
  • The circuit breaker caps the bill at 4 percent of income (5 percent when income is up to $58,200) and defers what is left.

Once you hold the senior exclusion you reapply only if you move to a new permanent residence. The circuit breaker is different and must be renewed every year. Disabled applicants attach a certificate from a North Carolina physician or a government agency. If the recipient dies, the person required to list the property tells the office.

The bill goes to whoever owned the parcel on January 1, and the county calls payment at closing the cleanest way to avoid trouble.

  1. Ask the Tax Office for the current balance before you sign a contract.
  2. If this year's tax is not yet due, the office accepts a prepayment based on the prior year's bill.
  3. Agree with the buyer on proration. That is a private deal, and the Tax Office does not calculate it.
  4. Have the closing attorney pay what is owed from your proceeds.

Under Session Law 2006-106 a seller is released from liability for tax assessed on property that was transferred before the bill went past due. The collector can still pursue whoever owns the parcel on the past-due date, so settle it at closing anyway. A cash sale skips lender payoff steps, but the tax still has to be settled.

A title search can turn up two more things. Unpaid demolition assessments from Winston-Salem, Kernersville or the county are billed through the tax office, and if they stay unpaid the parcel can head toward foreclosure. Tax foreclosures are run by an outside attorney, with sales at noon at 175 N. Chestnut Street and upset bids of at least 5 percent more and no less than $750 (G.S. 45-21.27).

Plan around three dates. September 1 is when the bill is due. January 5 is the last day to pay without interest. June 1 is the cutoff for relief applications. If you list in spring, your bill for the year is probably still open, and the buyer's lender will want to see it settled or prepaid.

Bring your parcel number and the most recent bill when you call 336-703-2300. The staff can tell you the balance, whether a payment agreement is in place and whether any demolition assessment is attached to the parcel. If an outside foreclosure attorney already has the file, the same line connects you to the foreclosure liaison.
Forsyth County has 401,718 residents as of July 1, 2025, and 184,703 housing units across 407.85 square miles of land.

faqs.q: What rate applies to Forsyth County bills for fiscal year 2027?
faqs.a: The county rate is 55.40 cents per $100 of assessed value. Town and fire district levies are added, and the rate sheet prints 1.143 as the Winston-Salem total.

faqs.q: Where is the Forsyth County Tax Office?
faqs.a: At 201 North Chestnut Street in Winston-Salem, open weekdays from 8 a.m. until 5 p.m. The main line is 336-703-2300. Mail payments to PO Box 82, Winston-Salem, NC 27102.

faqs.q: When does a Forsyth County bill turn delinquent?
faqs.a: After January 5 following the September 1 due date. Interest of 2 percent applies for January, then three-fourths of one percent for each later month.

faqs.q: Can a tax foreclosure in Forsyth County be stopped?
faqs.a: Yes, by paying all taxes, interest and fees. Ask for the foreclosure liaison at 336-703-2300 to get the balance, since an outside attorney runs the case.

faqs.q: Must I renew the senior exclusion each year in Forsyth County?
faqs.a: No, unless your permanent residence changes. Tell the office if income climbs above $38,800 or the disability ends. The circuit breaker is the exception and needs a new application every year.
